sections.plain:
Moves NEPA's definitions from section 111 to a new section 3 and expands them. New terms include agency chief environmental review and permitting officers, eNEPA technologies, key permitting agencies, a 20-page record of stakeholder engagement, record of decision, and statement of purpose and need.

The bill lists 14 kinds of action that are not major federal actions and so fall outside NEPA. A project whose only federal involvement is a loan or loan guarantee is out. So are routine administrative actions under $10 million, and repair or replacement of lifeline infrastructure that adds no more than 20 percent capacity.

The list also excludes geothermal observation test projects, transmission upgrades under new Federal Power Act section 216A(b), covered Natural Gas Act pipeline work, actions another agency already evaluated, and Army Corps continuing-authority or environmental-infrastructure projects with a federal share of $50 million or less.

vs.current:
NEPA section 111 (added by the Fiscal Responsibility Act of 2023) lists seven exclusions: non-federal actions with no or minimal federal funding or involvement, general revenue sharing, loans and loan guarantees where the agency lacks sufficient control over their use, SBA loan guarantees, enforcement actions, extraterritorial actions, and non-discretionary actions.

The bill makes a loan or loan guarantee an exclusion on its own terms when it is the only federal involvement. It covers grants and cost-share awards where the agency lacks predominant control. It adds seven exclusions: routine administrative actions up to $10 million, lifeline infrastructure repair, geothermal test projects, in-corridor transmission work, in-corridor gas pipeline work, actions another agency already reviewed, and Corps projects with a federal share up to $50 million.
vs.speed: The SPEED Act (sec. 2(f)) added grants and cost-share awards to the financial-assistance exclusion, required 'complete' agency control before funding counts, excluded Farm Service Agency loans and actions already reviewed by another agency, and said federal funding alone cannot make an action major. It also defined 'reasonably foreseeable' effects as those with a close causal relationship to the project. The Senate bill has no such definition in NEPA and no limit on the scope of effects an agency may study; its list of excluded actions is longer.
vs.epra: EPRA 2024 did not amend NEPA definitions.

sections.plain:
Rewrites NEPA section 107, the core of the review process. Environmental assessments are due in 1 year and environmental impact statements in 2 years, measured from the earlier of the agency's determination or its notice that the application is complete. A record of decision follows a final EIS within 45 days. Agencies in the review must decide all authorizations within 90 days, and agencies outside it within 120 days.

Lead agency designation gets a clock, with the CEQ Chairman resolving disputes within 21 days by a final, unreviewable decision. The Chairman can also order a resolution of interagency disputes, and that order counts as full compliance with any interagency consultation obligation under federal law.

The lead agency must drop any alternative that does not meet the purpose and need or the goals of a non-federal sponsor. Agencies need not consider science published after the notice of intent. Public scoping comment periods run 45 to 60 days, or 75 with the sponsor's consent.

If an agency defies a Chairman's dispute order and a deadline is missed, then after 30 days its permitting officers and senior executives must spend at least half their workweek on the overdue review. Once any deadline is 60 days overdue, the agency head may not travel more than 25 miles from the duty station until the document or permit issues. The Secretary of Defense is exempt. Project sponsors can sue over missed deadlines. The court must rule within 120 days and can order a decision within 60 days.

vs.current:
The Fiscal Responsibility Act of 2023 set the 2-year EIS and 1-year EA deadlines, page limits of 150 pages for an EIS and 75 for an EA (both kept), and a sponsor's right to petition a court, which can order the agency to act within 90 days.

New here: the clock no longer starts at the notice of intent. A record of decision is due 45 days after the EIS and all permits within 90 or 120 days. Agencies need not consider science published after the notice of intent. The CEQ Chairman settles lead-agency and interagency disputes with final, unreviewable orders, and lead-agency disputes take 21 days, down from 40. It had no CEQ dispute orders and no sanctions on agency staff or agency heads.
vs.epra: EPRA 2024 did not rewrite NEPA section 107; its deadlines were project-specific (energy leasing, rights-of-way).

sections.divh: COMMITTEE ON ENVIRONMENT AND PUBLIC WORKS
sections.plain:
Adds a judicial review section to NEPA. Suits challenging an authorization on NEPA grounds must be filed within 150 days. The party must allege an actual or imminent injury amounting to direct harm. Where a comment period was offered, the party must also have filed a sufficiently detailed comment. The federal court of appeals for the circuit where the project sits gets original and exclusive jurisdiction, with random judge assignment.

If a court finds a NEPA violation, the only remedy is remand without vacatur or injunction, with a fix deadline of no more than 180 days. The permit stays in effect and the project can proceed during the remand. A preliminary injunction is available only for a likely violation of a law other than NEPA or the National Historic Preservation Act.

Courts must give substantial deference to agencies on the scope and content of environmental documents. No NEPA suit may be brought over an action on tribal trust lands unless the tribe itself sues or effects reach beyond trust lands. No suit may rest on an omission from the list described in section 3(22)(B) of NEPA as amended.

quotes.why: Remand is the only remedy; a court cannot vacate or enjoin.

quotes.t: a claim shall be barred unless the claim— “(1) is filed not later than 150 days
quotes.why: The 150-day filing deadline.

vs.current: NEPA has no limitations period of its own, so the general 6-year limit on suits against the United States applies, with 2 years for FAST-41 covered projects and 150 days for highway and transit projects. There is no statutory prior-comment rule, cases start in district court, and courts can vacate or enjoin an approval.
vs.speed: The SPEED Act (sec. 3) had the same core: 150 days, prior comment, direct harm, substantial deference, remand without vacatur or injunction, a 180-day fix deadline, and the tribal trust carve-out. Differences: the House bill barred challenges to the creation of categorical exclusions, required courts to rule within 180 days of receiving the record and appeals within another 180, and applied its remand rule to court orders entered before enactment. The Senate bill drops those three, moves cases to the courts of appeals with random assignment, lets construction continue during a remand in express terms, and allows a preliminary injunction when a different federal law is likely violated.
vs.epra: EPRA 2024 (sec. 101) set a 150-day limit for energy and mineral project authorizations and a 180-day remand deadline. It did not require prior comment, did not change standing, and left courts their ordinary remedies. That section survives as section 2201 of this bill.

sections.h: Clean Water Act permitting and State certification
sections.divh: COMMITTEE ON ENVIRONMENT AND PUBLIC WORKS
sections.plain:
Rewrites Clean Water Act section 401 state certification. Certification is limited to water quality requirements. A state may deny only on clear and convincing evidence that no condition could make the project comply, and may impose only conditions that are necessary, least burdensome, and consistent with the federal permit.

The process gets a prefiling meeting, a defined complete application, a 3-day receipt acknowledgment, a 90-day completeness notice, and a review period of up to 1 year that can be extended only if the applicant asks in writing and the certifying authority agrees in writing. Silence is a waiver. Denials must name the specific water quality requirement violated. On judicial review the burden of proof falls on the state by clear and convincing evidence.

For interstate gas pipelines and bulk-power transmission lines, certification covers only direct point source discharges and must be decided within 9 months.

Rewrites section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act. An 'adverse effect' must be reasonably foreseeable and must directly alter a historic property. Temporary alterations are excluded. Visual, atmospheric and audible effects are excluded unless they directly and significantly diminish the property. An 'undertaking' excludes projects whose only federal tie is a loan, guarantee or grant, the non-federal parts of a project, minor repairs, permit renewals and post-approval operations.

The process gets deadlines: 30 days to decide whether a project is an undertaking, 60 days for the agency's report, 90 days for a determination, then 60 days of consultation, 45 days for Advisory Council comments and 30 days for a final decision. note.label: Earlier bill
note.text: The Ratepayer Protection Act (H.R. 9340) would ask state regulators to consider making data centers of 100 megawatts or more pay the full incremental cost of upgrades, including after they leave, with financial assurance before construction. States would not have to adopt it. It passed the House 417-3 on September 16, 2026, and the Senate rejected cloture 57-43 on September 30. BAAJA section 228 uses similar terms but makes them binding at 20 megawatts, and section 2107(a) adds an embedded-cost charge for transmission. Harvard's Ari Peskoe called the House bill's consider standard 'largely symbolic', since Congress cannot force state regulators to act, and called BAAJA's data center rules 'an improvement on the status quo'.

bills.label: Data center bills
bills.intro: BAAJA's data center and load-growth rules beside the federal bills that would regulate large computing loads, transmission pricing, and interconnection speed. EPRA 2024 and the SPEED Act did not address data center ratepayer rules or non-firm transmission service. Each cell links to the text it summarizes.

versions.label: Current policy
versions.sub: The White House Ratepayer Protection Pledge (March 2026) and FERC's June 18, 2026 show cause orders. FERC set no large-load rule.

versions.label: Ratepayer Protection Act (H.R. 9340)
versions.sub: Evans (R-Colo.) and Castor (D-Fla.). House-passed text, September 16, 2026. Senate cloture failed September 30; vote sources are in the large-load comparison note.

versions.sub: Heinrich (D-N.M.), August 2026. In committee; a unanimous-consent request failed September 17.

rows.topic: Who is covered

policy.text: The Pledge: seven hyperscalers and AI companies, later joined by governors, developers and power providers. FERC's June 2026 orders: the six regional grid operators.
policy.quote: President Trump is calling on the leading United States hyperscalers and AI companies to build, bring, or buy all of the energy needed for building and operating data centers

rpa.text: Data centers with 100 MW or more of peak demand at one site or campus, contracting after enactment. The introduced bill covered any 100 MW load; committee narrowed it.
rpa.quote: require electric energy primarily to operate information technology infrastructure and related systems pertaining to data storage and computational applications and services

grid_savings.text: Any new or expanded non-residential load of 150 MW or more at one interconnection, counting affiliated sites and phases. Not limited to data centers.
grid_savings.quote: has an aggregate requested or projected peak electric demand of not less than 150 megawatts behind a single point of interconnection

pftp.text: Data centers drawing more than 50 MW, counting same-owner facilities in one utility area. Crypto mines are defined separately.
pftp.quote: has an energy demand greater than 50 megawatts

grid_act.text: Private data centers of 20 MW or more, existing or planned within 5 years. Federal data centers excluded.
grid_act.quote: with a power demand of 20 megawatts or more that is not owned, operated, or maintained

senate.text: Section 228: data centers and high-density computing, including crypto mining, of 20 MW or more at one site or at commonly controlled sites, counting phased buildouts. Section 2107(a) pricing: any computational load on the bulk-power system, no size threshold. Ancillary computing at other commercial or industrial facilities is excluded from section 228.

ts.t: Section 228: data centers and high-density computing, including crypto mining, of 20 MW or more at one site or at commonly controlled sites, counting phased buildouts.
Section 2107(a) pricing: any computational load on the bulk-power system, no size threshold.
Ancillary computing at other commercial or industrial facilities is excluded from section 228.

rows.topic: Binding or optional

policy.text: Mostly voluntary. The Pledge creates no legal duty. FERC's June 18 orders find grid operators' tariffs may be unjust and make them justify or rewrite them. No final FERC rule.
policy.quote: The Ratepayer Protection Pledge and the commitments embodied therein effectuate the national policy of the United States.

rpa.text: Optional. A PURPA standard each state must consider within 1 year and decide within 2. States need not adopt it.
rpa.quote: shall commence consideration under section 111, or set a hearing date for consideration

grid_savings.text: Binding. New Federal Power Act section 224 gives FERC jurisdiction over large-load interconnection; final rule within 1 year.
grid_savings.quote: the Commission shall issue a final rule, applicable to each transmitting utility, establishing standards and procedures for the interconnection of covered large loads

pftp.text: Mixed. FERC must order transmission cost tariffs (120 days) and a data center queue rule (180 days). The rate class is a PURPA standard states must consider.
pftp.quote: the Commission shall issue a rule requiring all covered interconnection entities to create, for the purpose of addressing reliability and affordability concerns from new data center loads

grid_act.text: Binding prohibition enforced by DOE, with penalties of at least $1 million a day.
grid_act.quote: a covered entity may not build, own, operate, or maintain a data center unless the data center derives all of its energy

senate.text: Binding. Section 228 is a federal floor in the Federal Power Act. Section 2107(a) orders FERC to revise its 1994 pricing policy in 270 days, propose a rule 270 days later and finish within a year.

ts.t: Binding.
Section 228 is a federal floor in the Federal Power Act. Section 2107(a) orders FERC to revise its 1994 pricing policy in 270 days, propose a rule 270 days later and finish within a year.

rows.topic: Cost of serving the load

policy.text: Pledge signers say they will pay for the new generation and grid upgrades their data centers need. Retail costs otherwise follow state rate cases.
policy.quote: Companies will pay for all new power delivery infrastructure upgrades required to service their data centers

rpa.text: Rates recover from the data center the full incremental cost of generation, transmission or distribution upgrades needed to serve it.
rpa.quote: shall be designed to recover from the large-load customer the full, incremental cost of any generation, transmission, or distribution upgrade necessary to serve the load of such large-load customer

grid_savings.text: The load pays all interconnection and direct-assignment costs. Network upgrades are charged to it and credited back against its transmission bills, as for generators. Generation and distribution are not covered.
grid_savings.quote: directly assigned to, and fully borne by, the applicable covered large-load customer

pftp.text: Data centers pay local transmission upgrades that exist only because of them. States must consider a rate class that recovers the full cost of upgrades.
pftp.quote: allocate to each interconnecting data center local transmission upgrade costs that, but for the existence of the data center, would not be needed

grid_act.text: No cost allocation rule. New data centers must be off the grid; existing ones must show they do not raise rates or pay credits.
grid_act.quote: will not increase the electrical rates paid by ratepayers

senate.text: No incremental cost of serving a covered load (generation, storage, transmission, distribution) may be recovered from other customers.

ts.t: No incremental cost of serving a covered load (generation, storage, transmission, distribution) may be recovered from other customers.

rows.topic: Transmission pricing

policy.text: FERC's 1994 transmission pricing policy allows the higher of embedded cost or incremental expansion cost for a service, rather than their sum. Separate lines may be priced on different bases.

rpa.text: Transmission upgrades fall under the state standard. No FERC role and no embedded-cost charge.
rpa.quote: any generation, transmission, or distribution upgrade necessary to serve the load of such large-load customer

grid_savings.text: FERC classifies and allocates facilities under interconnection rules adapted for loads. A load may fund regional lines in exchange for transmission rights.

rows.now: FERC Order No. 1920 requires transmission providers to consider advanced technologies (dynamic line ratings, power flow control, topology optimization) in regional planning, but does not compel utilities to build them.

rows.topic: Statutory wholesale market access for behind-the-meter power

rows.topic: Device-level metering and inverter telemetry
rows.now: FERC Order No. 2222 left metering and telemetry rules to individual RTO compliance filings and distribution utilities, without a statutory rule guaranteeing use of device-level or inverter equipment.

rows.now: EIA Form 861 collects utility sales by broad commercial and industrial sectors, without separate reporting on data center or computing power demand.
